title: Oracle Interval Partitioning Example by Month (Step by Step)
description: Oracle interval partitioning example by month: create the table, see auto-created SYS_P partitions, rename them, use PARTITION FOR and avoid ORA-14758.

Please check: (1) SYS_P numbers and the HIGH_VALUE text in the outputs are illustrative; (2) the exact INTERVAL column text in USER_PART_TABLES (shown as NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH')); (3) the error raised when inserting a NULL key (I wrote ORA-14300 for 19c; the docs only say NULL is not allowed) the exact error raised for DATE '9999-12-01' on a monthly table (docs say it causes an error but give no code); (4) the SET INTERVAL () / SET INTERVAL (...) sequence then DROP of p_before_2026 succeeds; (5) the rename PL/SQL block (LONG high_value in a cursor FOR loop) compiles and runs; (6) ORA-14300 wording differs in newer releases (26ai shows 'partitioning key ... is beyond the calculated exclusive upper interval bound ...'). data.text: Interval partitioning is a form of range partitioning where Oracle creates new partitions for you. You define one starting range partition and an interval, such as INTERVAL (NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH')), and every time a row arrives for a month that has no partition yet, the database creates that partition automatically. No more month-end jobs that add partitions, and no more inserts failing because nobody added next month's partition.

This tutorial builds a monthly interval-partitioned orders table step by step. You will see which partitions Oracle creates, how to find and rename the system-generated ones, how to query and drop a partition by date, and the errors people hit in real projects.
How interval partitioning works

With plain range partitioning, every partition has a fixed upper bound written in VALUES LESS THAN. If a row is inserted above the highest bound and there is no MAXVALUE partition, the insert fails with ORA-14400: inserted partition key does not map to any partition. Someone has to add partitions ahead of time.
Interval partitioning removes that chore. The table has two sections:

items.content: Range section: the partitions you wrote in CREATE TABLE. The high value of the last one is called the transition point.
Interval section: everything above the transition point. Oracle creates a partition here only when the first row for that interval is inserted.

data.text: The boundaries of interval partitions are fixed by arithmetic from the transition point, not by when data arrives. If the transition point is 1 January 2026 and the interval is one month, the July 2026 partition always covers 1 July to 31 July, even if no June partition exists yet. Empty months simply have no partition.

Oracle names each automatically created partition SYS_Pn, where n is a number the database picks. You can rename them later, and you can always refer to one by a value it contains using PARTITION FOR (...).

content: You add them with ADD PARTITION
ORA-14400 unless a MAXVALUE partition exists

data.title: Licensing
data.text: Interval partitioning has been available since Oracle 11g. Partitioning is a separately licensed option of Oracle Enterprise Edition, so check your licence before using it on a production database.
Sample setup: a monthly orders table
Create an orders table partitioned by order_date. It has one range partition for everything before 2026, and monthly interval partitions after that.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id     NUMBER        NOT NULL,
  customer_id  NUMBER        NOT NULL,
  order_date   DATE          NOT NULL,
  amount       NUMBER(10,2)  NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT orders_pk PRIMARY KEY (order_id)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date)
INTERVAL (NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH'))
(
  PARTITION p_before_2026 VALUES LESS THAN (DATE '2026-01-01')
);
data.caption: Monthly interval-partitioned table

data.text: The transition point is 1 January 2026. NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH') returns an INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH value of one month, which becomes the width of each new partition. Making order_date NOT NULL matters, as you will see in the mistakes section.
Now insert five orders. Note there is no order in March 2026.

data.caption: Sample rows

data.text: None of these inserts fails. The December 2025 order goes into the range partition. The others land in partitions for January, February and April 2026, which Oracle creates as the rows arrive.
Step 1: see which partitions Oracle created
Query USER_TAB_PARTITIONS. The INTERVAL column tells you whether a partition belongs to the interval section (YES) or the range section (NO).

data.code:
SELECT partition_name,
       partition_position,
       interval,
       high_value
  FROM user_tab_partitions
 WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS'
 ORDER BY partition_position;
data.caption: List the partitions of ORDERS

data.text: Four partitions exist. There is no partition with a high value of 1 April, because no March order was inserted. The SYS_P numbers on your database will be different; they are generated by Oracle and are only guaranteed to be unique. HIGH_VALUE is a LONG column holding the bound as an expression, which is why it looks like a TO_DATE call.
To check the interval defined on the table itself, query USER_PART_TABLES:

data.code:
TABLE_NAME  PARTITIONING_TYPE  INTERVAL
----------  -----------------  ---------------------------
ORDERS      RANGE              NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH')
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The partitioning type is still RANGE. Interval partitioning is an extension of range partitioning, and the INTERVAL column is what tells you the table creates partitions automatically.
Step 2: a late row fills the gap
Insert a March order now:

data.code:
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (6, 105, DATE '2026-03-10', 1200);
COMMIT;

data.text: Run the USER_TAB_PARTITIONS query again. A new partition for March appears at position 4, and the April partition moves to position 5. The new partition gets a higher SYS_P number than April because it was created later, so never assume the number order matches the date order. Always sort by partition_position or by the high value.
Step 3: work with a partition by date using PARTITION FOR

System-generated names are awkward in scripts because they differ between databases (development, test, production). PARTITION FOR solves this: you give any value that falls inside the partition, and Oracle finds it.
Query one month

data.caption: Read only the January 2026 partition

data.text: The value 15 January is not stored anywhere in the table. It only identifies the partition whose range contains it. Date display depends on your NLS_DATE_FORMAT setting.

data.title: You rarely need PARTITION FOR in application queries
data.text: A normal filter such as WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' AND order_date < DATE '2026-02-01' lets the optimizer prune to the same single partition. Use PARTITION FOR for maintenance work and ad hoc checks.
Rename a system-generated partition

data.code:
ALTER TABLE orders
  RENAME PARTITION FOR (DATE '2026-01-01') TO p_2026_01;

data.text: Renaming only changes the name. The partition stays in the interval section, so its INTERVAL column still shows YES.
Step 4: rename all new partitions automatically

Many teams want readable names like P_2026_02. The block below reads each SYS_P partition, turns its HIGH_VALUE expression into a real date with dynamic SQL, and renames it after the month it holds. You can schedule it with DBMS_SCHEDULER to run daily.

data.code:
DECLARE
  l_high DATE;
BEGIN
  FOR p IN (SELECT partition_name, high_value
              FROM user_tab_partitions
             WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS'
               AND interval = 'YES'
               AND partition_name LIKE 'SYS\_P%' ESCAPE '\')
  LOOP
    -- high_value is text like TO_DATE(' 2026-03-01 ...')
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ' || p.high_value || ' FROM dual'
      INTO l_high;

    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'ALTER TABLE orders RENAME PARTITION '
      || p.partition_name || ' TO P_'
      || TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(l_high, -1), 'YYYY_MM');
  END LOOP;
END;
/
data.caption: Rename SYS_P partitions to P_YYYY_MM

data.text: The high value is the exclusive upper bound, so ADD_MONTHS(l_high, -1) gives the first day of the month the partition actually contains. A partition with high value 1 March 2026 becomes P_2026_02. The LIKE 'SYS\_P%' filter skips partitions already renamed, so running the block twice is safe.

data.code:
PARTITION_NAME  POSITION  INTERVAL
--------------  --------  --------
P_BEFORE_2026          1  NO
P_2026_01              2  YES
P_2026_02              3  YES
P_2026_03              4  YES
P_2026_04              5  YES
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Step 5: drop old months (data retention)
Interval partitioning pairs well with a retention policy: old months are removed with a fast metadata operation instead of a big DELETE.

data.caption: Drop the January 2026 partition

data.text: UPDATE INDEXES keeps the primary key index usable. The orders_pk index is a global, non-partitioned index, and without this clause dropping a partition that contains rows leaves it UNUSABLE, which breaks inserts and lookups until it is rebuilt. Local index partitions are dropped along with the table partition.
Why you cannot drop the first partition
Now try to drop the range partition:

data.code: ALTER TABLE orders DROP PARTITION p_before_2026;
ORA-14758: Last partition in the range section cannot be dropped
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Oracle needs at least one range partition to anchor the interval arithmetic, so the highest range partition can never be dropped. The fix is to move the transition point up first. Setting the interval again converts every existing interval partition into a range partition:

data.caption: Move the transition point, then drop

data.text: After the first statement the table is plain range partitioned, and the existing monthly partitions become range partitions with their current bounds. The second statement switches interval partitioning back on, with the new transition point at the top of the highest partition. p_before_2026 is no longer the last range partition, so it can be dropped. Check USER_TAB_PARTITIONS afterwards: the INTERVAL column now shows NO for the converted partitions.

One side effect: the lowest remaining partition has no lower bound, so any older row inserted later (say a December 2025 order) will go into it. That is usually fine for a retention policy, but be aware of it if old data can still arrive.
Other interval types: daily, weekly, yearly and numbers
The interval expression must match the partitioning key. Use NUMTOYMINTERVAL for months and years, NUMTODSINTERVAL for days, and a plain number for NUMBER keys.

data.code:
-- one partition per day
PARTITION BY RANGE (log_time)
INTERVAL (NUMTODSINTERVAL(1, 'DAY'))
(PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN (DATE '2026-01-01'))

-- one partition per week (7 days from the transition point)
INTERVAL (NUMTODSINTERVAL(7, 'DAY'))

-- one partition per year
INTERVAL (NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'YEAR'))

-- one partition per 100000 ids on a NUMBER key
PARTITION BY RANGE (payment_id)
INTERVAL (100000)
(PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN (100000))
data.caption: Interval clause variations

data.text: Weekly partitions start on the weekday of your transition point, because each one is exactly 7 days after the previous bound. If you want weeks to start on Monday, pick a Monday as the transition point.
Convert an existing range-partitioned table
You do not need to rebuild a range-partitioned table to get automatic partitions. SET INTERVAL converts it in place:

The current highest bound becomes the transition point. This only works when the table has no MAXVALUE partition, because an interval table cannot have one. If yours has an empty MAXVALUE partition, drop it first.
Common mistakes
Allowing NULL in the partitioning key

The documentation says you cannot use NULL values for the partitioning key of an interval-partitioned table. A row with a NULL key has no interval to go to, so the insert fails (in 19c it is reported as ORA-14300: partitioning key maps to a partition outside maximum permitted number of partitions). Declare the key column NOT NULL so the error is clear and happens at the right place.
A bad date creates a far-future partition

A typo such as year 2206 instead of 2026 is not rejected. Oracle quietly creates a partition 180 years ahead, and it stays there until you drop it. Two limits make bad values fail outright. A table can have at most 1024K - 1 (1,048,575) partitions, counted in interval positions from the transition point, so on a daily table a key far in the future fails with ORA-14300. And the documentation warns that a value such as DATE '9999-12-01', often used as a "no end date" marker, fails on a monthly table because the partition's upper bound would be 1 January 10000, which a DATE cannot store. Validate dates in the application or with a check constraint.

data.code:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_date_chk
  CHECK (order_date < DATE '2100-01-01');
data.caption: Block absurd future dates

data.text: Hard-coding SYS_P names in scripts
SYS_P2042 on test will be something else on production. Use PARTITION FOR or rename partitions first.
Trying ADD PARTITION

You cannot explicitly add a partition to an interval-partitioned table. The partition appears when data arrives. If you need an empty partition to exist in advance, for example before an exchange partition load, the documentation uses LOCK TABLE orders PARTITION FOR (DATE '2026-06-01') IN SHARE MODE to materialise it.
Changing the interval at the wrong boundary

Switching a daily table to monthly with SET INTERVAL fails with ORA-14767: Cannot specify this interval with existing high bounds if the highest partition bound is not on a month boundary, such as 30 January. Make sure a partition ends on the first of a month before changing.

data.title: Global indexes and partition maintenance
data.text: Dropping, truncating or merging partitions marks global indexes UNUSABLE unless you add UPDATE INDEXES (or UPDATE GLOBAL INDEXES). Always include it on tables used by applications.
Performance tips

items.content: Filter on the raw key column. Write order_date >= DATE '2026-02-01' AND order_date < DATE '2026-03-01' rather than TRUNC(order_date) = ... or TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') = .... Wrapping the key in a function can stop the optimizer from pruning partitions.
Check pruning in the plan. In DBMS_XPLAN output, look for PARTITION RANGE SINGLE or PARTITION RANGE ITERATOR with a narrow Pstart/Pstop, not PARTITION RANGE ALL.
Prefer local indexes where the query always filters by the partition key. They are maintained per partition and survive drops and truncates without rebuilds.

Pick a sensible interval. Daily partitions on a low-volume table produce thousands of tiny segments with little benefit. Monthly is a common middle ground; choose based on how you query and how you purge.
Gather statistics on new partitions. A fresh partition starts with no statistics. Make sure your stats job (or incremental statistics) covers new partitions.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between range and interval partitioning in Oracle?

Interval partitioning is range partitioning where Oracle adds new partitions automatically above the transition point. With range partitioning you add each partition yourself, or inserts beyond the last bound fail with ORA-14400.
Can I use interval partitioning on a VARCHAR2 column?
No. The single partitioning key must be NUMBER, DATE, FLOAT or TIMESTAMP. If your dates are stored as text, convert them to a real DATE column (or a virtual column) first.
How do I find the partition name for a date in an interval partitioned table?
Query USER_TAB_PARTITIONS ordered by partition_position and read HIGH_VALUE, or skip the name entirely and use PARTITION FOR (DATE '2026-02-10') in your statement.
Can I have a MAXVALUE partition with interval partitioning?
No. A MAXVALUE partition would catch every future row, so there would be nothing left for interval partitions. Oracle rejects it.
Does interval partitioning work with subpartitions?
Yes, as the top level. Oracle supports interval-range, interval-hash and interval-list composite partitioning. Interval partitioning is not supported at the subpartition level.
Summary

items.content: Interval partitioning = range partitioning plus automatic partition creation above the transition point.
Define at least one range partition and an INTERVAL expression; no MAXVALUE.
One key column only: NUMBER, DATE, FLOAT or TIMESTAMP, declared NOT NULL.
Find partitions in USER_TAB_PARTITIONS; INTERVAL = 'YES' marks auto-created ones.
Use PARTITION FOR (value) instead of hard-coded SYS_P names.
Add UPDATE INDEXES when dropping or truncating partitions.
To drop the first range partition, run SET INTERVAL () then set the interval again.
Guard against typo dates that create far-future partitions.

linkedin.post:
Your monthly job that adds next month's partition failed, and now every insert throws ORA-14400.
Oracle interval partitioning removes that job entirely. You define one starting partition and an interval, and Oracle creates each new partition when the first row for it arrives.

What to know before you use it:
→ Add INTERVAL (NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1, 'MONTH')) after PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date)
→ Only one key column, of type NUMBER, DATE, FLOAT or TIMESTAMP, and no MAXVALUE partition
→ New partitions get names like SYS_P2041. Never hard-code them; use PARTITION FOR (DATE '2026-01-15') instead
→ The last range partition cannot be dropped (ORA-14758). Run SET INTERVAL () and then set the interval again to move the transition point
→ A typo date like 2206 quietly creates a partition 180 years ahead, so validate dates

slides.title: Create a monthly table
slides.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id   NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date DATE NOT NULL,
  amount     NUMBER(10,2)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date)
INTERVAL (NUMTOYMINTERVAL(1,'MONTH'))
(PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN
   (DATE '2026-01-01'));

slides.title: Find the auto-created partitions
slides.body: New partitions get names like SYS_P2041. The INTERVAL column in USER_TAB_PARTITIONS is YES for them. Sort by partition_position, not by name.
slides.code:
SELECT partition_name, interval
  FROM user_tab_partitions
 WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS'
 ORDER BY partition_position;

slides.title: Use PARTITION FOR, not SYS_P names
slides.code:
ALTER TABLE orders
  RENAME PARTITION
  FOR (DATE '2026-01-01')
  TO p_2026_01;

ALTER TABLE orders
  DROP PARTITION
  FOR (DATE '2026-02-01')
  UPDATE INDEXES;

points: One key column: NUMBER, DATE, FLOAT or TIMESTAMP
No MAXVALUE partition, and keep the key NOT NULL
